common_name: Wrexham Buttercup Red Hot Poker (Tall Golden-Yellow Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; sharp drainage is essential year-round, especially through winter, to prevent crown rot.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, giving this Award of Garden Merit selection room to form a substantial clump of grassy, arching foliage. Wrexham Buttercup sends up tall, sturdy spikes in early to midsummer that open bright orange-tinted buds maturing to a clear, glowing buttercup-yellow, holding that solid gold color for weeks rather than fading through the red-to-cream gradient typical of many red hot pokers. The dense flower torches attract hummingbirds and bees over a long bloom window, and the strong stems rarely need staking. In colder parts of its range, gather and tie the foliage over the crown before the first hard freeze and mulch heavily for winter protection, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Ice Queen Red Hot Poker (Tall Late-Season Ivory-Green Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical, especially in winter, since red hot poker rots in waterlogged conditions.

directions: Ice Queen is among the tallest and latest-blooming kniphofias in general cultivation, holding its statuesque, pale creamy-yellow-green flower spikes on sturdy stems well above the grassy foliage from late summer into fall, after most other red hot pokers have finished. The soft, unusual coloring pairs beautifully with late-season asters, ornamental grasses, and dark-foliaged companions, and the flowers continue to draw late-migrating hummingbirds and pollinators. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, allow ample room for its large mature size, and protect the crown with a dry winter mulch in colder zones. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Christmas Cheer Red Hot Poker (Compact Autumn-Blooming Kniphofia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; good drainage is critical, especially in winter, since red hot poker rots in waterlogged conditions.

directions: Christmas Cheer is an older, long-proven kniphofia selection valued for its late, festively colored display, sending up dense torches of vivid coral-orange-red that soften to creamy yellow at the base as they age, held over compact clumps of arching, grass-like foliage from late summer well into autumn. Its comparatively modest height keeps it useful toward the middle of the border, where it extends hummingbird interest later into the season than most summer-blooming red hot pokers. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun, tie the foliage over the crown and mulch deeply before hard frost in colder zones, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Crater Lake Blue Speedwell (Compact Gentian-Blue Veronica)

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; this Award of Garden Merit selection forms a low, spreading mound that is easily divided.

directions: Crater Lake Blue forms a low, dense mound of small, deep green leaves that all but disappears beneath a flush of vivid, saturated gentian-blue flowers in late spring, one of the most intensely colored blues among the shorter garden speedwells. Its tidy, spreading habit makes it a strong choice for the front of a sunny border, rock gardens, or edging where a compact pop of true blue is wanted. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, shear lightly after the main bloom flush to tidy the mound and encourage a scattering of repeat flowers, and divide every two to three years in spring to keep clumps vigorous.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; because it is grown chiefly for its foliage pattern, propagate only by division to keep the variegation true.

directions: This variegated sport of the species forms a low rosette of glossy leaves edged in creamy white, providing bright, textural groundcover well before the same loose spikes of pale ice-blue flowers with darker veining appear in late spring. The cream margins are most vivid in light shade or morning sun, since strong afternoon sun can scorch the pale leaf edges in hotter climates. Plant in evenly moist, well-drained soil, remove any shoots that revert to solid green to preserve the variegation, and divide every three to four years in spring as clumps become congested.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Icicle brings crisp white flower spikes to the classic upright spike speedwell habit, forming a tidy mound of dark green foliage topped by dense, tapering racemes from early to midsummer. The pure white color makes it an easy mixer in perennial borders, standing out against silver foliage and cooling down hot-colored companions, and its short, sturdy stems rarely require staking. Grow in full sun in average, well-drained soil, deadhead spent spikes to encourage a secondary flush of bloom, and divide every two to three years in spring to keep clumps dense and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Waterperry Blue spreads by trailing stems that root as they go, quickly forming a low mat.

directions: Waterperry Blue is a low, mat-forming speedwell whose small rounded leaves emerge bronze-purple in cool weather and deepen further through winter before greening up in summer heat, giving it multi-season foliage interest beyond its bloom period. Loose sprays of soft lavender-blue flowers cover the mat in mid to late spring, slightly later and softer in tone than the more vivid Georgia Blue. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat tight, and use it along path edges, in rock gardens, or cascading over low walls where its trailing habit and colorful winter foliage can be appreciated up close.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plugs in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this species dislikes wet winter soil more than most other speedwells.

directions: Trehane is grown as much for its foliage as its flowers, forming a low, woody-based mat of bright golden-chartreuse leaves that hold their color through the growing season and turn warm bronze tones in cool weather. Short racemes of clear blue flowers appear in late spring and early summer, standing out sharply against the gold foliage. The brightest leaf color develops with a little relief from the hottest afternoon sun, so light shade in warmer climates prevents scorching, while full sun in cooler regions keeps the color most vivid. Plant in lean, fast-draining soil, shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense, and divide congested patches every few years in spring.
